   266		// complete, it'll unreference through invoking [Batch.Unref].
   267		//
   268		// When the committer of a batch indicates intent to recycle a Batch through
   269		// calling [Batch.Reset] or [Batch.Close], the lifecycle atomic is read. If
   270		// an outstanding reference remains, it's unsafe to reuse Batch.data yet. In
   271		// [Batch.Reset] the caller wants to reuse the [Batch] immediately, so we
   272		// discard b.data to recycle the struct but not the underlying byte slice.
   273		// In [Batch.Close], we set a special high bit [batchClosedBit] on lifecycle
   274		// that indicates that the user will not use [Batch] again and we're free to
   275		// recycle it when safe. When the commit pipeline eventually calls
   276		// [Batch.Unref], the [batchClosedBit] is noticed and the batch is
   277		// recycled.
   278		lifecycle atomic.Int32

   281	// batchClosedBit is a bit stored on Batch.lifecycle to indicate that the user
   282	// called [Batch.Close] to release a Batch, but an open reference count
   283	// prevented immediate recycling.
   284	const batchClosedBit = 1 << 30

   286	// TODO(jackson): Hide the wal.RefCount implementation from the public Batch interface.

   288	// Ref implements wal.RefCount. If the WAL writer may need to read b.data after
   289	// it returns, it invokes Ref to increment the lifecycle's reference count. When
   290	// it's finished, it invokes Unref.
   291	func (b *Batch) Ref() {
   292		b.lifecycle.Add(+1)
   293	}
   294	
   295	// Unref implemets wal.RefCount.
   296	func (b *Batch) Unref() {
   297		if v := b.lifecycle.Add(-1); (v ^ batchClosedBit) == 0 {
   298			// The [batchClosedBit] high bit is set, and there are no outstanding
   299			// references. The user of the Batch called [Batch.Close], expecting the
   300			// batch to be recycled. However, our outstanding reference count
   301			// prevented recycling. As the last to dereference, we're now
   302			// responsible for releasing the batch.
   303			b.lifecycle.Store(0)
   304			b.release()
   305		}
   306	}

   433	// BatchCommitStats exposes stats related to committing a batch.
   434	//
   435	// NB: there is no Pebble internal tracing (using LoggerAndTracer) of slow
   436	// batch commits. The caller can use these stats to do their own tracing as
   437	// needed.

   439		// TotalDuration is the time spent in DB.{Apply,ApplyNoSyncWait} or
   440		// Batch.Commit, plus the time waiting in Batch.SyncWait. If there is a gap
   441		// between calling ApplyNoSyncWait and calling SyncWait, that gap could
   442		// include some duration in which real work was being done for the commit
   443		// and will not be included here. This missing time is considered acceptable
   444		// since the goal of these stats is to understand user-facing latency.
   445		//
   446		// TotalDuration includes time spent in various queues both inside Pebble
   447		// and outside Pebble (I/O queues, goroutine scheduler queue, mutex wait
   448		// etc.). For some of these queues (which we consider important) the wait
   449		// times are included below -- these expose low-level implementation detail
   450		// and are meant for expert diagnosis and subject to change. There may be
   451		// unaccounted time after subtracting those values from TotalDuration.
   452		TotalDuration time.Duration
   453		// SemaphoreWaitDuration is the wait time for semaphores in
   454		// commitPipeline.Commit.
   455		SemaphoreWaitDuration time.Duration
   456		// WALQueueWaitDuration is the wait time for allocating memory blocks in the
   457		// LogWriter (due to the LogWriter not writing fast enough). At the moment
   458		// this is duration is always zero because a single WAL will allow
   459		// allocating memory blocks up to the entire memtable size. In the future,
   460		// we may pipeline WALs and bound the WAL queued blocks separately, so this
   461		// field is preserved for that possibility.
   462		WALQueueWaitDuration time.Duration
   463		// MemTableWriteStallDuration is the wait caused by a write stall due to too
   464		// many memtables (due to not flushing fast enough).
   465		MemTableWriteStallDuration time.Duration
   466		// L0ReadAmpWriteStallDuration is the wait caused by a write stall due to
   467		// high read amplification in L0 (due to not compacting fast enough out of
   468		// L0).
   469		L0ReadAmpWriteStallDuration time.Duration

   471		// syncing and closing the old WAL and creating (or reusing) a new one.

   473		// CommitWaitDuration is the wait for publishing the seqnum plus the

   476		CommitWaitDuration time.Duration
   477	}

  1386		*iter = batchIter{
  1387			batch: b,
  1388			iter:  b.index.NewIter(o.GetLowerBound(), o.GetUpperBound()),

  1390			// key iterator. Filtering point keys within the batch iterator can
  1391			// cause pathological behavior where a batch iterator advances
  1392			// significantly farther than necessary filtering many batch keys that
  1393			// are not visible at the batch sequence number. Instead, the merging
  1394			// iterator enforces bounds.

  1396			// For example, consider an engine that contains the committed keys
  1397			// 'bar' and 'bax', with no keys between them. Consider a batch
  1398			// containing keys 1,000 keys within the range [a,z]. All of the
  1399			// batch keys were added to the batch after the iterator was
  1400			// constructed, so they are not visible to the iterator. A call to
  1401			// SeekGE('bax') would seek the LSM iterators and discover the key
  1402			// 'bax'. It would also seek the batch iterator, landing on the key
  1403			// 'baz' but discover it that it's not visible. The batch iterator would
  1404			// next through the rest of the batch's keys, only to discover there are
  1405			// no visible keys greater than or equal to 'bax'.
  1406			//
  1407			// Filtering these batch points within the merging iterator ensures that
  1408			// the batch iterator never needs to iterate beyond 'baz', because it
  1409			// already found a smaller, visible key 'bax'.
  1410			snapshot: base.SeqNumMax,
  1411		}
  1412	}

  1414	func (b *Batch) newRangeDelIter(o *IterOptions, batchSnapshot base.SeqNum) *keyspan.Iter {
  1415		// Construct an iterator even if rangeDelIndex is nil, because it is allowed

  1422	func (b *Batch) initRangeDelIter(_ *IterOptions, iter *keyspan.Iter, batchSnapshot base.SeqNum) {
  1423		if b.rangeDelIndex == nil {
  1424			iter.Init(b.comparer.Compare, nil)
  1425			return
  1426		}
  1427	
  1428		// Fragment the range tombstones the first time a range deletion iterator is
  1429		// requested. The cached tombstones are invalidated if another range
  1430		// deletion tombstone is added to the batch. This cache is only guaranteed
  1431		// to be correct if we're opening an iterator to read at a batch sequence
  1432		// number at least as high as tombstonesSeqNum. The cache is guaranteed to
  1433		// include all tombstones up to tombstonesSeqNum, and if any additional
  1434		// tombstones were added after that sequence number the cache would've been
  1435		// cleared.
  1436		nextSeqNum := b.nextSeqNum()
  1437		if b.tombstones != nil && b.tombstonesSeqNum <= batchSnapshot {
  1438			iter.Init(b.comparer.Compare, b.tombstones)
  1439			return
  1440		}
  1441	
  1442		tombstones := make([]keyspan.Span, 0, b.countRangeDels)
  1443		frag := &keyspan.Fragmenter{
  1444			Cmp:    b.comparer.Compare,
  1445			Format: b.comparer.FormatKey,
  1446			Emit: func(s keyspan.Span) {
  1447				tombstones = append(tombstones, s)
  1448			},
  1449		}
  1450		it := &batchIter{
  1451			batch:    b,
  1452			iter:     b.rangeDelIndex.NewIter(nil, nil),
  1453			snapshot: batchSnapshot,
  1454		}
  1455		fragmentRangeDels(frag, it, int(b.countRangeDels))
  1456		iter.Init(b.comparer.Compare, tombstones)
  1457	
  1458		// If we just read all the tombstones in the batch (eg, batchSnapshot was
  1459		// set to b.nextSeqNum()), then cache the tombstones so that a subsequent
  1460		// call to initRangeDelIter may use them without refragmenting.
  1461		if nextSeqNum == batchSnapshot {
  1462			b.tombstones = tombstones
  1463			b.tombstonesSeqNum = nextSeqNum
  1464		}
  1465	}

  1467	func fragmentRangeDels(frag *keyspan.Fragmenter, it internalIterator, count int) {
  1468		// The memory management here is a bit subtle. The keys and values returned
  1469		// by the iterator are slices in Batch.data. Thus the fragmented tombstones
  1470		// are slices within Batch.data. If additional entries are added to the
  1471		// Batch, Batch.data may be reallocated. The references in the fragmented
  1472		// tombstones will remain valid, pointing into the old Batch.data. GC for
  1473		// the win.
  1474	
  1475		// Use a single []keyspan.Key buffer to avoid allocating many
  1476		// individual []keyspan.Key slices with a single element each.
  1477		keyBuf := make([]keyspan.Key, 0, count)
  1478		for kv := it.First(); kv != nil; kv = it.Next() {
  1479			s := rangedel.Decode(kv.K, kv.InPlaceValue(), keyBuf)
  1480			keyBuf = s.Keys[len(s.Keys):]
  1481	
  1482			// Set a fixed capacity to avoid accidental overwriting.
  1483			s.Keys = s.Keys[:len(s.Keys):len(s.Keys)]
  1484			frag.Add(s)
  1485		}
  1486		frag.Finish()
  1487	}

  1784	func (i *batchIter) SeekGE(key []byte, flags base.SeekGEFlags) *base.InternalKV {
  1785		// Ignore TrySeekUsingNext if the view of the batch changed.
  1786		if flags.TrySeekUsingNext() && flags.BatchJustRefreshed() {
  1787			flags = flags.DisableTrySeekUsingNext()
  1788		}
  1789	
  1790		i.err = nil // clear cached iteration error
  1791		i.prefix = nil
  1792		ikey := i.iter.SeekGE(key, flags)
  1793		for ikey != nil && ikey.SeqNum() >= i.snapshot {
  1794			ikey = i.iter.Next()
  1795		}
  1796		if ikey == nil {
  1797			i.kv = base.InternalKV{}
  1798			return nil
  1799		}
  1800		i.kv.K = *ikey
  1801		i.kv.V = base.MakeInPlaceValue(i.value())
  1802		return &i.kv
  1803	}

  1805	func (i *batchIter) SeekPrefixGE(prefix, key []byte, flags base.SeekGEFlags) *base.InternalKV {
  1806		// SeekGE clears i.prefix, so any TrySeekUsingNext path inside it operates
  1807		// without prefix gating. Re-apply prefix afterward and check the result.

  2017			// correct sequence number will be set later. But it is correct when the
  2018			// batch is being replayed from the WAL.

  2236		return true

    19	// InterleavingIter wraps a base.InternalIterator (points) and a
    20	// keyspan.FragmentIterator (spans) and implements the iterv2.Iter interface.
    21	//
    22	// Given an overall [startKey, endKey) range, it partitions the key space into
    23	// contiguous spans (from the fragment iterator, plus synthesized empty gap
    24	// spans) and emits synthetic boundary keys when crossing span boundaries
    25	// during Next/Prev.
    26	type InterleavingIter struct {
    27		cmp       *base.Comparer
    28		pointIter base.InternalIterator
    29		spanIter  keyspan.FragmentIterator
    30	
    31		// [startKey, endKey) is the static key range for this iterator. The
    32		// wrapped iterators are assumed to only return keys within this range (no
    33		// key comparisons are performed to enforce it). These bounds are used as
    34		// fallback gap boundaries when lower/upper are not set.
    35		startKey []byte
    36		endKey   []byte
    37	
    38		// lower and upper are optional dynamic bounds that restrict the iteration
    39		// range within [startKey, endKey). Unlike startKey/endKey, these are
    40		// enforced via key comparisons. When set, First/Last panic (the caller
    41		// must use SeekGE/SeekLT instead). Nil means unbounded in that direction.
    42		lower []byte
    43		upper []byte
    44	
    45		// pointKV is the last KV returned by pointIter. This is also the last KV
    46		// returned by this iterator, unless the last KV returned was a boundary key
    47		// (atBoundary=true); in the latter case, pointKV is the next point in the
    48		// direction of iteration.
    49		pointKV *base.InternalKV
    50	
    51		// span is the current position of spanIter (the last result of a spanIter
    52		// operation). If inSpan is true, the current position of this iterator is
    53		// inside this span; otherwise span is the next span in the direction of
    54		// iteration.
    55		span *keyspan.Span
    56	
    57		// dir is +1 for forward, -1 for backward (and 0 for unpositioned).
    58		dir int8
    59		// inSpan indicates whether the current position is inside span. When inSpan is true,
    60		// the presentedSpan Boundary matches span.End (forward iteration) or span.Start
    61		// (backward iteration).
    62		inSpan bool
    63		// atBoundary indicates if the last returned key was a boundary key.
    64		atBoundary bool
    65		// presentedSpan is the iterv2.Span presented by this iterator via Span().
    66		presentedSpan Span
    67		// kv is used to avoid allocations when returning boundary keys.
    68		kv     base.InternalKV

    72		tmpBuf []byte

    77	// Init initializes the InterleavingIter.
    78	//
    79	// spanIter may be nil, in which case the iterator behaves as if there are no
    80	// spans (the entire key range is one empty gap).

    82	// There are two sets of bounds:
    83	//
    84	// [startKey, endKey) defines the static key range owned by this iterator.
    85	// Everything returned by the wrapped iterators is assumed to already be within
    86	// this range (no key comparisons are performed to enforce it). These are used
    87	// to determine gap span boundaries when no dynamic bounds are set. In the level
    88	// iterator, startKey/endKey are derived from file boundaries and divide the
    89	// entire keyspace exactly between InterleavingIters. Forward seeks at keys
    90	// below startKey are equivalent doing the seek at startKey. Similarly, SeekLT
    91	// at a key above endKey is equivalent to SeekLT(endKey).
    92	//
    93	// lower and upper are optional dynamic bounds; nil means unbounded in that
    94	// direction. They restrict the iteration range within [startKey, endKey) and
    95	// are enforced via key comparisons. When set, First/Last cannot be used (the
    96	// caller must use SeekGE/SeekLT instead); they are equivalent to SetBounds

    19	// constructRangeKeyIter constructs the range-key iterator stack, populating
    20	// i.rangeKey.rangeKeyIter with the resulting iterator.
    21	func (i *Iterator) constructRangeKeyIter() {
    22		i.rangeKey.rangeKeyIter = i.rangeKey.iterConfig.Init(
    23			i.comparer, i.seqNum, i.opts.LowerBound, i.opts.UpperBound,
    24			&i.hasPrefix, &i.prefixOrFullSeekKey, false /* internalKeys */, &i.rangeKey.rangeKeyBuffers.internal)
    25	
    26		if i.opts.DebugRangeKeyStack {
    27			// The default logger is preferable to i.opts.getLogger(), at least in the
    28			// metamorphic test.
    29			i.rangeKey.rangeKeyIter = keyspan.InjectLogging(i.rangeKey.rangeKeyIter, base.DefaultLogger)
    30		}
    31	
    32		// If there's an indexed batch with range keys, include it.
    33		if i.batch != nil {
    34			if i.batch.batch.index == nil {
    35				// This isn't an indexed batch. We shouldn't have gotten this far.
    36				panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("creating an iterator over an unindexed batch"))
    37			} else {
    38				// Only include the batch's range key iterator if it has any keys.
    39				// NB: This can force reconstruction of the rangekey iterator stack
    40				// in SetOptions if subsequently range keys are added. See
    41				// SetOptions.
    42				if i.batch.batch.countRangeKeys > 0 {
    43					i.batch.batch.initRangeKeyIter(&i.opts, &i.batch.rangeKeyIter, i.batch.batchSeqNum)
    44					i.rangeKey.iterConfig.AddLevel(&i.batch.rangeKeyIter)
    45				}
    46			}
    47		}
    48	
    49		if !i.batchOnlyIter {
    50			// Next are the flushables: memtables and large batches.
    51			if i.readState != nil {
    52				for j := len(i.readState.memtables) - 1; j >= 0; j-- {
    53					mem := i.readState.memtables[j]
    54					// We only need to read from memtables which contain sequence numbers older
    55					// than seqNum.
    56					if logSeqNum := mem.logSeqNum; logSeqNum >= i.seqNum {
    57						continue
    58					}
    59					if rki := mem.newRangeKeyIter(&i.opts); rki != nil {
    60						i.rangeKey.iterConfig.AddLevel(rki)
    61					}
    62				}
    63			}
    64	
    65			current := i.version
    66			if current == nil {
    67				current = i.readState.current
    68			}
    69			// Next are the file levels: L0 sub-levels followed by lower levels.
    70	
    71			// Add file-specific iterators for L0 files containing range keys. We
    72			// maintain a separate manifest.LevelMetadata for each level containing only
    73			// files that contain range keys, however we don't compute a separate
    74			// L0Sublevels data structure too.
    75			//
    76			// We first use L0's LevelMetadata to peek and see whether L0 contains any
    77			// range keys at all. If it does, we create a range key level iterator per
    78			// level that contains range keys using the information from L0Sublevels.
    79			// Some sublevels may not contain any range keys, and we need to iterate
    80			// through the fileMetadata to determine that. Since L0's file count should
    81			// not significantly exceed ~1000 files (see L0CompactionFileThreshold),
    82			// this should be okay.
    83			if !current.RangeKeyLevels[0].Empty() {
    84				// L0 contains at least 1 file containing range keys.
    85				// Add level iterators for the L0 sublevels, iterating from newest to
    86				// oldest.
    87				for j := len(current.L0SublevelFiles) - 1; j >= 0; j-- {
    88					iter := current.L0SublevelFiles[j].Iter()
    89					if !containsAnyRangeKeys(iter) {
    90						continue
    91					}
    92	
    93					li := i.rangeKey.iterConfig.NewLevelIter()
    94					li.Init(
    95						i.ctx,
    96						i.opts.SpanIterOptions(),
    97						i.cmp,
    98						i.newIterRangeKey,
    99						iter.Filter(manifest.KeyTypeRange),
   100						manifest.L0Sublevel(j),
   101						manifest.KeyTypeRange,
   102					)
   103					i.rangeKey.iterConfig.AddLevel(li)
   104				}
   105			}
   106	
   107			// Add level iterators for the non-empty non-L0 levels.
   108			for level := 1; level < len(current.RangeKeyLevels); level++ {
   109				if current.RangeKeyLevels[level].Empty() {
   110					continue
   111				}
   112				li := i.rangeKey.iterConfig.NewLevelIter()
   113				spanIterOpts := i.opts.SpanIterOptions()
   114				li.Init(i.ctx, spanIterOpts, i.cmp, i.newIterRangeKey, current.RangeKeyLevels[level].Iter(),
   115					manifest.Level(level), manifest.KeyTypeRange)
   116				i.rangeKey.iterConfig.AddLevel(li)
   117			}
   118		}
   119	}

   121	func containsAnyRangeKeys(iter manifest.LevelIterator) bool {
   122		for f := iter.First(); f != nil; f = iter.Next() {
   123			if f.HasRangeKeys {
   124				return true
   125			}
   126		}
   127		return false

   130	// Range key masking
   131	//
   132	// Pebble iterators may be configured such that range keys with suffixes mask
   133	// point keys with lower suffixes. The intended use is implementing a MVCC
   134	// delete range operation using range keys, when suffixes are MVCC timestamps.
   135	//
   136	// To enable masking, the user populates the IterOptions's RangeKeyMasking
   137	// field. The Suffix field configures which range keys act as masks. The
   138	// intended use is to hold a MVCC read timestamp. When implementing a MVCC
   139	// delete range operation, only range keys that are visible at the read
   140	// timestamp should be visible. If a range key has a suffix ≤
   141	// RangeKeyMasking.Suffix, it acts as a mask.
   142	//
   143	// Range key masking is facilitated by the keyspan.InterleavingIter. The
   144	// interleaving iterator interleaves range keys and point keys during combined
   145	// iteration. During user iteration, the interleaving iterator is configured
   146	// with a keyspan.SpanMask, implemented by the rangeKeyMasking struct below.
   147	// The SpanMask interface defines two methods: SpanChanged and SkipPoint.
   148	//
   149	// SpanChanged is used to keep the current mask up-to-date. Whenever the point
   150	// iterator has stepped into or out of the bounds of a range key, the
   151	// interleaving iterator invokes SpanChanged passing the current covering range
   152	// key. The below rangeKeyMasking implementation scans the range keys looking
   153	// for the range key with the largest suffix that's still ≤ the suffix supplied
   154	// to IterOptions.RangeKeyMasking.Suffix (the "read timestamp"). If it finds a
   155	// range key that meets the condition, the range key should act as a mask. The
   156	// span and the relevant range key's suffix are saved.
   157	//
   158	// The above ensures that `rangeKeyMasking.maskActiveSuffix` always contains the
   159	// current masking suffix such that any point keys with lower suffixes should be
   160	// skipped.
   161	//
   162	// There are two ways in which masked point keys are skipped.
   163	//
   164	//   1. Interleaving iterator SkipPoint
   165	//
   166	// Whenever the interleaving iterator encounters a point key that falls within
   167	// the bounds of a range key, it invokes SkipPoint. The interleaving iterator
   168	// guarantees that the SpanChanged method described above has already been
   169	// invoked with the covering range key. The below rangeKeyMasking implementation
   170	// of SkipPoint splits the key into prefix and suffix, compares the suffix to
   171	// the `maskActiveSuffix` updated by SpanChanged and returns true if
   172	// suffix(point) < maskActiveSuffix.
   173	//
   174	// The SkipPoint logic is sufficient to ensure that the Pebble iterator filters
   175	// out all masked point keys. However, it requires the iterator read each masked
   176	// point key. For broad range keys that mask many points, this may be expensive.
   177	//
   178	//   2. Block property filter
   179	//
   180	// For more efficient handling of braad range keys that mask many points, the
   181	// IterOptions.RangeKeyMasking field has an optional Filter option. This Filter
   182	// field takes a superset of the block-property filter interface, adding a
   183	// method to dynamically configure the filter's filtering criteria.
   184	//
   185	// To make use of the Filter option, the user is required to define and
   186	// configure a block-property collector that collects a property containing at
   187	// least the maximum suffix of a key within a block.
   188	//
   189	// When the SpanChanged method described above is invoked, rangeKeyMasking also
   190	// reconfigures the user-provided filter. It invokes a SetSuffix method,
   191	// providing the `maskActiveSuffix`, requesting that from now on the
   192	// block-property filter return Intersects()=false for any properties indicating
   193	// that a block contains exclusively keys with suffixes greater than the
   194	// provided suffix.
   195	//

    37	// recordQueue is a variable-size single-producer multiple-consumer queue. It
    38	// is not lock-free, but most operations only need mu.RLock. It needs a mutex
    39	// to grow the size, since there is no upper bound on the number of queued
    40	// records (which are all the records that are not synced, and will need to be
    41	// written again in case of failover). Additionally, it needs a mutex to
    42	// atomically grab a snapshot of the queued records and provide them to a new
    43	// LogWriter that is being switched to.
    44	type recordQueue struct {
    45		// Only held for reading for all pop operations and most push operations.
   120		// for writing, there is a guarantee that headTail is not being updated.
   121		//
   122		// head is most-significant 32 bits and tail is least-significant 32 bits.
   123		headTail atomic.Uint64
   124	
   125		consumerMu sync.Mutex
   126	
   127		// Access to buffer requires at least RLock.
   128		buffer []recordQueueEntry
   129	
   130		lastTailObservedByProducer uint32
   131	
   132		// Read requires RLock.
   133		writer *record.LogWriter
   134	
   135		// When writer != nil, this is the return value of the last call to
   136		// SyncRecordGeneralized. It is updated in (a) WriteRecord calls push, using
   137		// only RLock (since WriteRecord is externally synchronized), (b)
   138		// snapshotAndSwitchWriter, using Lock. (b) excludes (a).
   139		lastLogSize int64
   140	
   141		failoverWriteAndSyncLatency prometheus.Histogram
   142	}

   144	func (q *recordQueue) init(failoverWriteAndSyncLatency prometheus.Histogram) {
   145		*q = recordQueue{
   146			buffer:                      make([]recordQueueEntry, initialBufferLen),
   147			failoverWriteAndSyncLatency: failoverWriteAndSyncLatency,
   148		}
   149	}

   151	// NB: externally synchronized, i.e., no concurrent push calls.
   152	func (q *recordQueue) push(
   153		p []byte,
   154		opts SyncOptions,
   155		refCount RefCount,
   156		writeStart crtime.Mono,
   157		latestLogSizeInWriteRecord int64,
   158		latestWriterInWriteRecord *record.LogWriter,
   159	) (index uint32, writer *record.LogWriter, lastLogSize int64) {
   160		ht := q.headTail.Load()
   161		h, t := unpackHeadTail(ht)
   162		n := int(h - t)
   163		m := len(q.buffer)
   164		if m == n {
   165			// Full
   166			m = 2 * n
   167			newBuffer := make([]recordQueueEntry, m)
   168			for i := int(t); i < int(h); i++ {
   169				newBuffer[i%m] = q.buffer[i%n]
   170			}
   171			q.mu.Lock()
   172			q.buffer = newBuffer
   173			q.mu.Unlock()
   174		}
   175		q.mu.RLock()
   176		q.buffer[int(h)%m] = recordQueueEntry{
   177			p:          p,
   178			opts:       opts,
   179			refCount:   refCount,
   180			writeStart: writeStart,
   181		}
   182		// Reclaim memory for consumed entries. We couldn't do that in pop since
   183		// multiple consumers are popping using CAS and that immediately transfers
   184		// ownership to the producer.
   185		for i := q.lastTailObservedByProducer; i < t; i++ {
   186			q.buffer[int(i)%m] = recordQueueEntry{}
   187		}
   188		q.lastTailObservedByProducer = t
   189		q.headTail.Add(1 << headTailBits)
   190		writer = q.writer

   300		writer *record.LogWriter,
   301		snapshotFunc func(firstIndex uint32, entries []recordQueueEntry) (logSize int64),

   303		q.mu.Lock()
   304		defer q.mu.Unlock()
   305		q.writer = writer
   306		h, t := unpackHeadTail(q.headTail.Load())
   307		n := h - t
   308		if n > 0 {
   309			m := uint32(len(q.buffer))
   310			b := make([]recordQueueEntry, n)
   311			for i := t; i < h; i++ {
   312				b[i-t] = q.buffer[i%m]
   313			}
   314			q.lastLogSize = snapshotFunc(t, b)

   326	func unpackHeadTail(ht uint64) (head, tail uint32) {
   327		const mask = 1<<headTailBits - 1
   328		head = uint32((ht >> headTailBits) & mask)
   329		tail = uint32(ht & mask)
